passage: In the university canteen in Delhi, Noor pushed her notes aside. "I can't study anymore today. I used up all my willpower in the stats test. It's science, na? Willpower is like a fuel tank." Hafsa, a psychology student, stirred her tea. "That's what I thought too. But today our professor showed us that when big labs across many countries repeated those willpower experiments, most found tiny effects or none." "So I'm not tired?" "No, you're tired. That's real. It's the fuel-tank part they're not sure about. Some studies even suggest people who believe willpower runs out feel more worn out." Noor frowned. "So what do I do?" Hafsa shrugged. "Maybe rest a bit, eat something, and try twenty minutes. See what happens."

qa.a: Hafsa takes Noor's tiredness seriously but doubts the fuel-tank explanation, since the repeated studies didn't confirm it.

qa.q: What does Hafsa suggest Noor try, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Rest a bit, eat something and try twenty minutes; it respects real tiredness without assuming willpower has simply run out.

qa.q: How might Noor feel hearing 'You're tired. That's real'?
qa.a: Noor may feel relieved to be believed, and curious that the explanation she trusted is less certain than she thought.

passage:
'Bhaiya, why are you ordering pizza? You said you'd cook,' Irfan said.
Abhinav dropped onto the sofa. 'I made decisions all day at the bank. My willpower's gone. Ego depletion. You study psychology, you should know.'
'I do know. That's the thing.' Irfan closed his laptop. 'We read about it this week. When they repeated the big studies with thousands of people, the effect almost disappeared.'
'So I'm making it up?'
'No, you're tired. Tiredness is real. But the "tank runs empty" idea is shaky. Some research says if you believe it runs out, you give up sooner.'
Abhinav squinted at him. 'So what's the real reason?'
'Honestly? Nobody's sure. Could be tiredness, boredom, or just not wanting to cook.'
Abhinav laughed. 'Fine. Pizza tonight. You cook tomorrow, professor.'

qa.q: What did Irfan say happened when the big studies were repeated?
qa.a: When they repeated them with thousands of people, the effect almost disappeared.

qa.q: Why might Irfan be careful to say 'you're tired, tiredness is real'?
qa.a: He doesn't want Abhinav to feel accused of making it up; he doubts the explanation, not his brother's tiredness.

qa.q: What choice could Abhinav make on tiring days, given the uncertainty?
qa.a: He could take the tiredness seriously without assuming his willpower is gone, perhaps planning a simple meal earlier in the day.

qa.q: How does Abhinav seem to take being corrected by Irfan?
qa.a: He squints, then laughs and teases Irfan as 'professor', taking the point in good humour while still ordering pizza.

grounding: At home, a psychology student questions his older brother's 'willpower is gone' claim, noting failed replications while accepting tiredness is real.

subtype: Skeptic of the fuel tank idea [Observer]
passage: I'm Nikita, final-year psychology, and I used to love the willpower-as-fuel idea. It explained everything: why I ate chips after exams, why I couldn't study after a long day. For our research methods project, my lab partner Tanuja and I read about the big replication, where dozens of labs ran the same depletion task. The pooled effect was close to zero. I was honestly annoyed. Tanuja said, "Maybe it's more complicated. Maybe what we believe about tiredness changes how tired we act." We ran a tiny class survey. People who agreed that "willpower runs out" reported giving up sooner. It proved nothing; it was just thirty students. But it changed how I talk about it. I'm still tired after exams. I just don't know exactly why anymore, and I'm okay with that.

qa.q: What did the big replication find when dozens of labs ran the same task?
qa.a: The pooled effect was close to zero.

qa.q: Why was Nikita honestly annoyed at first?
qa.a: The fuel idea had neatly explained Nikita's own habits, so losing it felt like losing a comfortable explanation.

qa.q: What makes Nikita's class survey useful, even though it proved nothing?
qa.a: It prompted a more careful view: tiredness is real, beliefs might matter, and thirty students can't settle the mechanism.

qa.q: How does Tanuja seem to see the failed replication differently from Nikita at first?
qa.a: Tanuja treats it as a puzzle to explore, that beliefs might shape tiredness, while Nikita first feels annoyed at losing a tidy idea.

grounding: A psychology student learns large replications failed to confirm depletion and that beliefs about tiredness may matter.

Tutorial note, Research Methods, week 9. Written by the course tutor.
Today Chetan told the group that the stats quiz after a long lab was impossible because "willpower runs out like petrol." Saurabh, who usually sits quietly at the back, said, "I believed that too. Then I read about the big replication studies with thousands of people. Most found tiny effects or none." Chetan frowned. "So I'm just lazy?" Saurabh shook his head. "No. You're tired, that's real. It's just that nobody's sure it works like a tank. Some studies suggest people who don't believe willpower runs out keep going longer." I was struck by how carefully he held both points. Next week I have asked Saurabh to lead ten minutes on what replications can and can't tell us.

qa.q: What did Saurabh say most of the big replication studies found?
qa.a: Most found tiny effects or none.

qa.q: Why did Chetan ask 'So I'm just lazy?'
qa.a: Chetan seems worried that without the petrol explanation, the tiredness becomes a character flaw; the fuel-tank idea had felt like a kind reason for struggling.

qa.q: What choice did the tutor make after the discussion, and why does it fit?
qa.a: The tutor asked Saurabh to lead ten minutes on what replications can and can't tell us, building on his balanced view instead of letting the class swing to a new certainty.

qa.q: How might Saurabh have felt answering Chetan's 'So I'm just lazy?'
qa.a: Saurabh probably felt careful and sympathetic, taking Chetan's tiredness seriously ('You're tired, that's real') while staying honest that the tank idea is doubtful.

grounding: A psychology student explains that large replications found weak depletion effects and beliefs may matter, while insisting tiredness is real.

subtype: Skeptic of the fuel tank idea [Observer]
passage:
Thursday night
Tanvir came back from the hospital internship at 9, dropped onto the bed and said, "Zero willpower left, Sudha. Tank empty." Then ordered fried momos and skipped the flashcards.
A month ago I'd have nodded. Today in cognitive psych, Ma'am showed us the huge multi-lab replication, dozens of labs, and the effect nearly vanished. Some people looked cheated. I felt weirdly curious.
Because Tanvir IS exhausted. I could see it in how slowly the shoelaces came undone. That part isn't fake. It's the tank story I'm not sure about anymore. Maybe believing the tank is empty makes it feel emptier? Maybe it's boredom?
Didn't lecture. Just asked if Tanvir wanted to do five cards together tomorrow morning instead. 🙂
- Sudha

qa.q: What time did Tanvir come back from the hospital internship?
qa.a: Tanvir came back at 9.

qa.q: How can you tell Sudha feels uncertain rather than convinced by either side?
qa.a: Sudha writes 'I'm not sure about anymore' and lists other possibilities like belief or boredom, while still insisting Tanvir's exhaustion is real.

qa.q: What choice did Sudha make instead of lecturing, and why might it work?
qa.a: Sudha offered to do five cards together in the morning, which respects Tanvir's tiredness and moves the hard task to a fresher time without an argument about theory.

qa.q: What would change for Tanvir if Sudha announced that the tank idea had been 'disproved'?
qa.a: Tanvir might hear it as 'you're not really tired' and feel dismissed after a long shift, and it would overstate the evidence, since the mechanism is uncertain rather than settled.

grounding: A psychology student learns that large replications failed to confirm depletion and wonders about belief and boredom, while treating a friend's tiredness as real.
